accepted.s: The recommendations for the reorganisation of the Indian Army after the Revolt of 1857 were associated with which commission?
accepted.x: The Peel Commission, constituted in 1859, recommended major changes in the composition, organisation and recruitment of the Indian Army.
accepted.tq: Identify the commission associated with a specific administrative measure.
accepted.sec: Army reorganisation - Peel Commission, ratio, artillery, recruitment

accepted.s: After the recommendations of the Peel Commission, the European-to-Indian ratio in the Bengal Army was changed from
accepted.x: The European-to-Indian ratio in the Bengal Army was altered from 1:5 to 1:2 after the Revolt of 1857.
accepted.tq: Track the direction of change between two numerical ratios.
accepted.sec: Army reorganisation - Peel Commission, ratio, artillery, recruitment

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the reorganisation of the British Indian Army after 1857:
1. Artillery was placed exclusively under European control.
2. Indians were barred from serving with heavy weapons.
3. Regiments were organised on caste, community and regional lines.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: All three statements are correct. The British retained artillery and heavy weapons for Europeans and organised other regiments to restrict unity and fraternisation among Indian soldiers.
accepted.tq: Check each administrative measure separately before selecting the combined code.
accepted.sec: Army reorganisation - Peel Commission, ratio, artillery, recruitment

accepted.s: Which one of the following was NOT a principal basis for organising regiments in the post-1857 British Indian Army?
accepted.x: Regiments were organised according to caste, community and region. A common national identity was contrary to the British policy of preventing cross-regional fraternisation.
accepted.tq: Find the option that reverses the stated purpose of an administrative policy.
accepted.sec: Army reorganisation - Peel Commission, ratio, artillery, recruitment

accepted.s: The recruitment policy of the British after the Revolt of 1857 increasingly favoured which groups as so-called “martial races”?
accepted.x: The British increasingly recruited Sikhs, Gurkhas and Pathans, describing them as martial races, while reducing dependence on recruits from Awadh and Bihar.
accepted.tq: Distinguish the favoured recruitment groups from the groups deliberately reduced.
accepted.sec: Army reorganisation - Peel Commission, ratio, artillery, recruitment

accepted.s: The “counterpoise” principle in the post-1857 army policy primarily meant
o: placing all artillery under Indian officers
recruiting soldiers exclusively from princely states
using divisions based on caste, community and region to prevent military unity
accepted.x: The counterpoise principle used social, regional and communal divisions within the army to prevent collective action and cross-regional fraternisation.
accepted.tq: Apply the underlying purpose of a policy to a short administrative situation.
accepted.sec: Army reorganisation - Peel Commission, ratio, artillery, recruitment

accepted.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched with the post-1857 recruitment policy?
o: Awadh and Bihar — preferred martial-race recruitment zones
Sikhs and Gurkhas — communities increasingly recruited by the British
Pathans and Rajputs — communities excluded from military service
Bengalis and Biharis — exclusive guardians of artillery
accepted.x: Sikhs and Gurkhas were among the communities increasingly recruited under the martial-races policy. Awadh and Bihar were comparatively disfavoured after 1857.
accepted.tq: Start with the sure community-policy association and eliminate reversed pairs.
accepted.sec: Army reorganisation - Peel Commission, ratio, artillery, recruitment

accepted.s: Who withdrew the Doctrine of Lapse and recognised the right of adoption by childless Indian rulers?
accepted.x: Lord Canning withdrew the Doctrine of Lapse and recognised adoption rights after 1857. This marked the abandonment of Dalhousie’s annexation policy.
accepted.tq: Use the ruler-policy trap by separating the policy’s originator from the person who ended it.
accepted.sec: Policy towards princes - adoption rights, end of annexation

accepted.s: The policy of annexation associated with Lord Dalhousie was officially abandoned after 1857 mainly through the recognition of
o: the election of rulers by legislative councils
the complete independence of princely states
the right of adoption by childless rulers
accepted.x: The British recognised the right of childless rulers to adopt heirs, thereby withdrawing the Doctrine of Lapse and ending the annexation policy associated with Dalhousie.
accepted.tq: Identify the constitutional-political consequence of a policy change.
accepted.sec: Policy towards princes - adoption rights, end of annexation

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements about the post-1857 policy towards Indian princes:
1. Princes were assured that their states would not ordinarily be annexed.
2. Their acceptance of British paramountcy was required.
3. They became subordinate allies and supports of British rule.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: All three statements are correct. The princes retained their states subject to British paramountcy and were converted into loyal subordinate allies of the Crown.
accepted.tq: Test the relationship between territorial assurance, paramountcy and political dependence.
accepted.sec: Policy towards princes - adoption rights, end of annexation

accepted.s: The description of Indian princes as “breakwaters to the storm” after the Revolt of 1857 is associated with
accepted.x: Lord Elgin described the loyal Indian princes as “breakwaters to the storm,” reflecting their role as supports of British rule after 1857.
accepted.tq: Match a distinctive phrase with its associated British official.
accepted.sec: Policy towards princes - adoption rights, end of annexation

accepted.s: Which of the following best describes the change in British policy towards Muslims after 1857?
o: The British transferred all administrative posts exclusively to Muslims.
The British consistently treated Muslims as their principal allies from the beginning.
The British initially blamed and targeted Muslims, but later cultivated them against the educated Hindu middle class.
The British abandoned all communal distinctions and promoted joint political representation.
accepted.x: The British initially held Muslims chiefly responsible for the revolt and adopted anti-Muslim measures, but later cultivated Muslim support against the rising educated Hindu middle class.
accepted.tq: Follow the chronological shift rather than selecting an absolute statement.
accepted.sec: Divide-and-rule and racial attitudes - Hindu-Muslim policy shift

accepted.s:
Arrange the following developments in the British policy after the Revolt of 1857 in the correct chronological order:
A. Initial anti-Muslim policy
B. Cultivation of Muslims against the educated Hindu middle class
C. Greater protection to zamindars and landlords
D. Abandonment of reforming zeal and social interference
accepted.x: The British first adopted an anti-Muslim posture, later cultivated Muslims against educated Hindus, protected landed interests and withdrew from social reform and interference.
accepted.tq: Arrange policy changes by their stated sequence from initial reaction to later consolidation.
accepted.sec: Divide-and-rule and racial attitudes - Hindu-Muslim policy shift

accepted.s: Which one of the following was NOT a feature of British policy towards social and landed interests after 1857?
o: Withdrawal from missionary and reforming activity
Continued aggressive interference in Indian social customs
Recognition of proprietary rights of zamindars and taluqdars
accepted.x: The British abandoned their earlier reforming zeal and adopted a policy of non-interference in social customs. They nevertheless protected landed interests and stepped back from missionary activity.
accepted.tq: Identify the reversed policy by testing the word “continued” against the historical shift.
accepted.sec: Divide-and-rule and racial attitudes - Hindu-Muslim policy shift

accepted.s: The reversal of the annexation of large estates in Awadh after 1857 resulted in zamindars and taluqdars being granted
o: exclusive authority over the British Indian Army
the right to reject British paramountcy
proprietary rights and transformed into a conservative loyalist class
accepted.x: In Awadh, zamindars and taluqdars were restored to proprietary rights and became a conservative and loyal landed class supporting British rule.
accepted.tq: Link an administrative concession to its political consequence.
accepted.sec: Divide-and-rule and racial attitudes - Hindu-Muslim policy shift

accepted.s: Which of the following correctly reflects British racial attitudes after the Revolt of 1857?
o: Indians were admitted freely to the highest administrative posts.
Rebels were generally tried through transparent constitutional procedures.
Racial arrogance hardened, rebels were publicly executed after mock trials, and Indians were excluded from higher posts.
Missionary activity was expanded as the central instrument of reconciliation.
accepted.x: Racial arrogance intensified after 1857. Rebels were publicly executed after mock trials, while Indians continued to be excluded from higher administrative positions.
accepted.tq: Prefer the precise combined description over options containing absolute reversals.
accepted.sec: Divide-and-rule and racial attitudes - Hindu-Muslim policy shift

accepted.s: The absence of Indians in the legislative council, as a lesson of the Revolt of 1857, was particularly criticised by
accepted.x: Sir Syed Ahmad Khan attributed part of the crisis to the absence of Indian opinion in the council, a concern addressed through later expansion and nomination of Indian members.
accepted.tq: Match the criticism of an institutional defect with its associated thinker.
accepted.sec: Indian Councils Act 1861 - link to 1857 lessons

accepted.s: The Indian Councils Act was passed on
accepted.x: The Indian Councils Act was passed on 1 August 1861 and marked an important beginning in the development of representative institutions in India.
accepted.tq: Distinguish the exact enactment date from nearby dates associated with related reforms.
accepted.sec: Indian Councils Act 1861 - link to 1857 lessons

accepted.s: Who among the following was NOT one of the first three Indians nominated by Canning to the expanded legislative council?
accepted.x: The first three Indians nominated by Canning were the Raja of Benaras, the Maharaja of Patiala and Sir Dinkar Rao. Sir Syed Ahmad Khan was not one of these three nominees.
accepted.tq: Find the outsider in a short list of named nominees.
accepted.sec: Indian Councils Act 1861 - link to 1857 lessons

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Indian Councils Act of 1861:
1. It enabled the Viceroy to nominate Indians as non-official members of his expanded legislative council.
2. It gave statutory recognition to Canning’s portfolio system.
3. It empowered the Viceroy to issue ordinances in an emergency.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: All three statements are correct. The Act incorporated Indian nomination, recognised the portfolio system introduced in 1859 and retained emergency ordinance-making power with the Viceroy.
accepted.tq: Test separate provisions of an Act before choosing the comprehensive code.
accepted.sec: Indian Councils Act 1861 - link to 1857 lessons

accepted.s: The portfolio system which received statutory recognition under the Indian Councils Act, 1861 had been introduced by Canning in
accepted.x: Canning introduced the portfolio system in 1859, and the Indian Councils Act of 1861 subsequently gave it statutory recognition.
accepted.tq: Separate the year of introduction from the year of statutory recognition.
accepted.sec: Indian Councils Act 1861 - link to 1857 lessons

accepted.s: The last Mughal emperor, Bahadur Shah II, was deported to
accepted.x: Bahadur Shah II was tried and exiled to Rangoon after the Revolt of 1857, where he died in 1862.
accepted.tq: Recall the precise place associated with exile rather than a nearby colonial location.
accepted.sec: End of the Mughal dynasty and East India Company

accepted.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the fate of the East India Company after 1857?
o: It retained political rule until 1874 and was then transferred to the Crown.
It was dissolved immediately in 1858 without any formal legal process.
It continued to rule India under the Crown until 1901.
It lost its rule under the Act of 1858 and was finally dissolved in 1874.
accepted.x: The Government of India Act, 1858 ended the Company’s political rule, while the East India Company was formally dissolved in 1874.
accepted.tq: Separate the year of loss of political power from the later year of formal dissolution.
accepted.sec: End of the Mughal dynasty and East India Company

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Bahadur Shah II was proclaimed Shahenshah-e-Hindustan by the rebels.
2. He was tried and exiled to Rangoon.
3. His exile marked the formal end of Mughal rule.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: All three statements are correct. The rebels proclaimed Bahadur Shah II as Shahenshah-e-Hindustan, after which the British tried and exiled him to Rangoon, ending the Mughal dynasty in practice and form.
accepted.tq: Combine title, consequence and sequence in a single historical event cluster.
accepted.sec: End of the Mughal dynasty and East India Company
